specAnchors.text: understand, in terms of bond enthalpy, the trend in reactivity of chloro-, bromo- and iodoalkanes

primer.text: Polarity promises fluorine, bond strength delivers iodine. This note weighs the two factors behind halogenoalkane reactivity, shows why the strongest polar bond is the hardest to break, and lands the ladder where substitution rates actually fall: iodide first, fluoride barely at all.

modules.title: Polarity and the reactivity puzzle
modules.opening: Electronegativity says fluoroalkanes should react fastest - the C-F bond is the most polar, so carbon looks most attackable. Reality inverts the prediction, and the deciding factor is bond strength, which wins over polarity every time.
keyPoints: The C-X bond is polar: carbon carries d+ and halogen d-, from the electronegativity difference.
Electronegativity falls down the group, so bond polarity also falls.
Polarity alone would suggest fluoroalkanes react quickest.
Bond strength is the greater factor and reverses the prediction.

low.restatement: The polarity ladder runs F strongest to I weakest, but the bond-enthalpy ladder runs the other way and carries more weight - so iodoalkanes, not fluoroalkanes, react fastest.
low.analogy: Two scoreboards disagree: polarity cheers fluorine, bond strength cheers iodine - and bond strength holds the tiebreaker.
low.examPointer: Name BOTH factors when explaining the reactivity trend, and state explicitly that bond enthalpy dominates polarity.

medium.restatement: The d+ carbon invites nucleophiles in every halogenoalkane; what differs is how easily the C-X bond can be broken once the nucleophile arrives. Weaker bonds (C-I) yield faster than strong ones (C-F).
medium.analogy: Every door looks open from outside (polarity), but the hinges differ (bond strength): the rustiest hinges swing first.
medium.examPointer: Answer 'why does the prediction fail?' with the bond-enthalpy override, not with a denial of polarity.

modules.title: Bond enthalpy decides the race
modules.opening: Substitution means breaking the carbon-halogen bond, so the bond energies write the reactivity ladder: C-I needs least energy and breaks first, C-F needs most and resists. Iodoethane with hydroxide shows the weakest bond falling fastest.
keyPoints: Every substitution must break the carbon-halogen bond, so bond energies explain the different reactivities.
The C-I bond demands the least break energy of the series, making it the weakest carbon-halogen bond.
The C-F bond requires the most energy and is the strongest carbon-halogen bond.
Iodoalkanes break heterolytically fastest: CH3CH2I + OH- -> CH3CH2OH + I-.

low.restatement: Rank the bonds by breakability - C-I easiest, then C-Br, C-Cl, C-F hardest - and the hydrolysis speed ladder follows exactly; the leaving halide departs with the bond's electron pair.
low.analogy: Four padlocks cut with increasing difficulty: iodine's is tin snips, fluorine's needs bolt cutters - the snips win every race.
low.examPointer: Tie the trend to the heterolytic departure: the pair goes with the halogen, and weaker bonds surrender their pair sooner.

medium.restatement: Bond enthalpy is the energy toll for the rate-determining break; down the group the bond lengthens and weakens, so iodoalkanes clear the toll first. The fluoroalkane's toll is so high it barely reacts at all.
medium.analogy: Toll booths on the substitution road: iodine charges pennies, fluorine charges a fortune - traffic flows accordingly.
medium.examPointer: Quote the iodoethane equation with OH- as the canonical fastest case.

glossary.definition: The unequal sharing of electrons in the C-X bond giving carbon d+ and halogen d-.
The energy required to break a bond; the decisive factor in halogenoalkane reactivity.
Bond breaking in which the electron pair departs with the halogen as X-.
